buildUp: You want to roll rather than walk, so you need two wheels in line and a seat between them, with pedals turning a crank under the rider.
The pedals turn far too slowly to drive the wheel directly, so a chain connects a large chainring at the cranks to a small sprocket at the rear wheel, multiplying the speed.
One ratio can't suit hills and flats, so there are two chainrings and eleven sprockets, with derailleurs that push the chain sideways from one to the next.
The frame must hold rider and wheels rigidly while weighing very little, so it's made of two triangles of thin tubes, with a fork that turns in the head tube to steer.
The wheels must be light, strong and round, so they're a thin rim hung from a hub by 32 tensioned spokes, with air-filled tyres to smooth out bumps and grip the road.
Finally, the rider needs to stop and control it, so cables run from the levers to rim brakes that squeeze pads onto the rims, with the front doing most of the stopping.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Let the rider's legs turn in a comfortable circle and use gears to match that circle to the road speed, while the machine itself wastes almost nothing. A chain drive about 95% efficient, rolling wheels instead of sliding feet, and a frame and wheels built from thin parts that work purely in tension and compression make it possible to go several times faster than running on less effort.

hardParts.title: A wheel that stays true
hardParts.why: Thirty-two thin spokes must each be tensioned to around 100 kgf so the rim stays round, straight and centred, and a change to one spoke shifts the load on its neighbours. On the rear wheel the cassette forces the hub's drive-side flange closer to the centre, so the drive-side spokes need much more tension than the others, making that wheel harder to build and more likely to break a spoke.

hardParts.title: Shifting gears under load
hardParts.why: The derailleur has to push a moving chain sideways by about 3.9 mm, the gap between sprockets, and let the sprocket's teeth pick it up cleanly, while the rider may be pushing hundreds of newtons through it. Ramps and shaped teeth on the sprockets, a sprung cage that takes up the slack in the chain, and very precise cable pulls are all needed to make each click land smoothly.

hardParts.title: Stiff where it matters, light everywhere else
hardParts.why: In a sprint, pedal forces of around 1,000 N try to twist the frame at the bottom bracket, and any flex there wastes energy and feels vague. The tubes near the bottom bracket and the chainstays are made wider and stiffer, while tubes elsewhere are thinned to under a millimetre in the middle, so the whole frame stays light without going soft.

principles.explanation: Your legs make the most power at a comfortable pedalling rate of roughly 80 to 100 turns a minute, whatever speed you're going. Gears let you keep that rate: with the 50-tooth ring and the 11-tooth sprocket, each pedal turn spins the back wheel about 4.5 times, covering roughly 9.5 metres; on the 34-tooth ring and 28-tooth sprocket it's only about 1.2 turns. It's the same idea as a lever: on a hill you trade distance for force, on the flat force for distance.
principles.title: Gears match legs to speed

principles.explanation: Rolling a well-pumped tyre on smooth tarmac takes little effort; pushing the air out of the way takes most of it. Air drag grows with the square of speed, and the power to beat it with the cube, so riding twice as fast takes about eight times the power against the wind. At about 30 km/h on the flat, roughly three-quarters or more of a rider's effort goes into air resistance, which is why racers crouch low on the drops.
principles.title: The air is the real enemy

principles.explanation: A frame of two triangles turns every load into simple pushing and pulling along each tube, which thin tubes are very good at resisting. A square frame of four rods joined at the corners can be pushed into a lozenge, but a triangle can't change shape without stretching or squashing one of its sides. The wheels go further: each spoke is a thin wire that only ever pulls, so the wheel is like a bicycle-sized suspension bridge, pre-stressed so the spokes stay tight under load.
principles.title: Triangles and tension

principles.explanation: A bicycle balances by steering, not by spinning wheels acting as gyroscopes. When the bike starts to lean, the rider, and partly the bike itself, steers the front wheel towards the lean, which moves the wheels back under the centre of mass, the same way you balance a broom on your hand by moving your hand. The fork's angle and the way the tyre's contact point trails behind the steering axis make the front wheel turn into a lean on its own, which is why a moving bike can roll along steadily with no hands.
principles.title: Why it stays upright

firstPrinciples.problem: Make the small power of human legs carry a rider many times faster than walking, on a machine light enough to carry yet strong enough to survive every pothole. A person can only put out a couple of hundred watts for any length of time, about as much as two old-fashioned 100-watt light bulbs, and legs work best turning at a fairly steady pace. That power has to work uphill and down, and the machine has to take hundreds of kilograms of force on every pothole. Every gram and every bit of friction comes straight out of the rider's legs.

questions.answer: Air drag rises with the square of speed, and since you also cover ground twice as fast, the power needed rises roughly with the cube. Doubling your speed takes roughly eight times the power against the air.
questions.question: Why is it so much harder to ride at 40 km/h than at 20 km/h, when it's only twice as fast?

questions.answer: They never push; they only pull. Every spoke is pre-tensioned, so the rim is hung from the hub, and the rider's weight just slightly relaxes the spokes at the bottom rather than compressing them.
questions.question: The spokes are thin wires that would bend if you pushed them. How do they hold up a heavy rider?

questions.answer: When you brake, your weight shifts forwards onto the front wheel, pressing it into the road and giving it more grip, while the rear wheel goes light. So the front can take much more braking force before skidding.
questions.question: Why do the front brakes do most of the stopping?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: A cyclist is one of the most efficient ways known for a human to travel, using far less energy per kilometre than walking. The bike gets there not with any single clever part but by wasting almost nothing: a drivetrain that loses only a few percent, wheels and a frame where every part only pushes or pulls, and gears that keep the rider's muscles at their sweet spot. About 8 kg of metal and rubber multiplies what your legs can do.

name: Road Bicycle
overview:
A bicycle is a machine for turning pedalling into forward motion as efficiently as possible. Your legs push the pedals round; the cranks turn the chainring, the chain carries that turn back to a sprocket on the rear wheel, and the rear wheel pushes the bike along. The ratio between the chainring and the sprocket you're in sets how far the bike travels per pedal stroke.

The frame is two triangles: the front triangle (top tube, down tube and seat tube) and the rear triangle (seat stays and chain stays). Triangles don't flex easily, so the frame stays stiff while weighing very little. The fork holds the front wheel and turns in the head tube when you steer; its angle and offset make the bike steady enough to ride no-handed.

Each wheel is a tension structure: thin spokes, pulled tight, hang the hub from the rim, so the wheel carries the rider's weight while weighing under a kilogram. Derailleurs shift the chain between sprockets for different gears, and rim brakes squeeze pads onto the wheel rims to stop.

parts.description: 25 mm clincher tyre pumped to around 6 bar; its tread is almost smooth, since road tyres grip through the rubber, not the pattern.

details.didYouKnow: Wider tyres at the same pressure do not have a bigger contact patch, just a shorter, wider one, which is partly why road tyres have crept from 23 mm to 25 mm and beyond.
details.howItWorks: The tyre's two edges, called beads, hook under lips on the rim, and the air in the tube pushes them outwards so they lock in place. Where the tyre meets the road it flattens into a small contact patch, and the rubber there grips by deforming into tiny bumps in the tarmac. The front tyre steers the bike, so a grippy, well-inflated front matters most in corners.
keyNumbers: Contact patch about the size of a thumbprint
details.madeOf: A woven nylon casing coated in rubber compound, with beads of steel wire or folding aramid fibre. The rubber blend trades grip against wear and rolling resistance.

parts.name: Front tyre

parts.description: Thin butyl tube that holds the air inside the tyre.

details.didYouKnow: Road bikes use slim Presta valves rather than car-style Schrader valves because they need a smaller hole in the narrow rim and seal better at high pressure.
details.howItWorks: The tube is a sealed rubber balloon that sits inside the tyre and is inflated through a valve poking through the rim. It does not carry the load itself: the air pressure stretches the tyre casing tight, and the casing does the work. If the tyre gets cut or pinched against the rim, the tube is what leaks.
details.madeOf: Butyl rubber, chosen because it holds air far better than natural rubber. Lighter versions use latex, which rolls more smoothly but loses air within a day or two.

parts.name: Front inner tube

parts.description: Aluminium hoop the tyre hooks onto; its sides double as the braking surface.

details.didYouKnow: Many rim-brake rims have a small wear groove or dot on the braking surface; when it disappears, the wall has grown too thin and the rim should be replaced.
details.howItWorks: The rim is the outer hoop that holds the tyre and anchors the far end of every spoke. Spoke nipples thread through holes in its inner wall, and tightening them pulls the rim true. On this bike its flat sidewalls are also the braking track, so the front brake pads rub directly on them, wearing them very slowly over the years.
keyNumbers: Braking track lasts typically many thousands of km
details.madeOf: Extruded aluminium alloy rolled into a hoop and joined by welding or a pinned sleeve. Aluminium is light, stiff and gives a consistent braking surface in the wet.

parts.name: Front rim

parts.description: Stainless spokes laced in a crossing pattern; under tension they hang the hub from the rim.

details.didYouKnow: A wheel does not stand on its bottom spokes; it hangs from the top ones, which is why a thin wire wheel can carry many times its own weight.
details.howItWorks: These 16 spokes run from the left hub flange to the rim and work only in tension, like the strings of a harp. When the wheel is loaded, the spokes at the bottom lose a little tension while the rest hold the hub suspended. On a rim-brake front wheel the hub is symmetrical, so these left spokes carry the same tension as the right ones.
keyNumbers: About 2 mm thick at the ends
details.madeOf: Cold-drawn stainless steel wire, often butted thinner in the middle to save weight and add a little stretch. Stainless resists rust and fatigue over millions of turns.

parts.name: Front spokes (left side)

parts.description: Stainless spokes laced in a crossing pattern; under tension they hang the hub from the rim.

details.didYouKnow: A wheel builder often tunes spoke tension by plucking the spokes and listening, since spokes at similar tension ring at a similar pitch.
details.howItWorks: The right-hand set of 16 spokes mirrors the left, crossing each other usually three times on the way to the rim so they can also handle braking forces through the rim. Because there is no chain or cassette at the front, the right side is not truly a drive side here and the two sides are dished evenly. Balancing their tension is what keeps the rim straight and centred.
keyNumbers: Spoke ends threaded about 2 mm diameter
details.madeOf: Stainless steel with threaded ends that screw into brass or aluminium nipples at the rim. Brass nipples are heavier but less likely to seize or crack.

parts.name: Front spokes (right side)

parts.description: Centre of the wheel: an axle on sealed ball bearings, with flanges the spokes hook into.

details.didYouKnow: The 100 mm front hub width has been the road bike standard for decades, so a front wheel from long ago will often still fit a modern rim-brake fork.
details.howItWorks: The hub body spins around a fixed axle on two sealed cartridge bearings, one near each flange. The quick release passes through the hollow axle and clamps its end caps into the fork dropouts. The front hub only has to support weight and braking loads, so it is simpler and lighter than the rear.
keyNumbers: Axle typically 9 mm for quick release
details.madeOf: A machined or forged aluminium shell with an aluminium or steel axle and steel ball bearings. Aluminium keeps the rotating weight low.

parts.name: Front hub

parts.description: Lever-operated skewer that clamps the wheel into the frame, removable without tools.

details.didYouKnow: The quick release was invented by Italian racer Tullio Campagnolo in the 1930s, reportedly after cold fingers stopped him undoing a wing nut during a race.
details.howItWorks: A thin rod runs through the hollow hub axle with a nut on one end and a cam lever on the other. Closing the lever turns the cam, which pulls the rod tight and squeezes the fork dropouts between the hub end caps. Small tabs on the fork ends, called lawyer lips, stop the wheel falling out if the lever is ever left open.
keyNumbers: Clamping force up to several hundred kgf
details.madeOf: A steel or titanium rod with an aluminium or steel lever and cam. Steel is strong enough to hold a big clamping force on a thin rod.

parts.name: Front quick release

parts.description: 25 mm clincher tyre pumped to around 6 bar; its tread is almost smooth, since road tyres grip through the rubber, not the pattern.

details.didYouKnow: Riders often swap a worn rear tyre for the front one and fit the new tyre at the front, because a front blowout or slide is the more dangerous one.
details.howItWorks: The rear tyre is built the same way as the front but works harder: it carries more of the rider's weight and transmits all the pedalling force to the road. That extra load and the scrubbing from drive torque make the centre of the tread wear flat much faster. It is usually run slightly firmer than the front for the same reason.
keyNumbers: Carries roughly 55 to 60% of the total weight
Often 0.3 to 0.5 bar firmer than the front
details.madeOf: Rubber compound over a nylon fabric casing, often with a puncture-resistant belt under the tread. The tread compound is a compromise between grip, wear and rolling speed.

parts.name: Rear tyre

parts.description: Thin butyl tube that holds the air inside the tyre.

details.didYouKnow: The two neat holes of a pinch flat are nicknamed a snakebite, because they look like fang marks.
details.howItWorks: Like the front tube, it is a thin balloon that pressurises the tyre so the casing can carry the load. The rear takes the heavier load, so it is the one most likely to get a pinch flat, where hitting an edge squashes the tyre and nips two small holes in the tube against the rim.
keyNumbers: Loses roughly 0.5 to 1 bar a week
Valve typically 48 to 60 mm long for shallow rims
details.madeOf: Butyl rubber for good air retention, with a brass or aluminium Presta valve. Butyl stretches enough to fit snugly but leaks very slowly.

parts.name: Rear inner tube

parts.description: Aluminium hoop the tyre hooks onto; its sides double as the braking surface.

details.didYouKnow: Rear rims are sometimes drilled off-centre so the spokes sit nearer the drive side, which lets the two sides run closer to equal tension.
details.howItWorks: The rear rim holds the tyre and the outer ends of all 32 spokes, but on the rear wheel the spokes pull it unevenly to make room for the cassette. Its sidewalls are braked on by the rear caliper, which does less of the stopping work than the front, so the rear braking surface usually wears more slowly.
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy extrusion, sometimes with an offset spoke bed on rear rims to help even out spoke tension. Aluminium gives a reliable braking surface and is easy to repair and true.

parts.name: Rear rim

parts.description: Stainless spokes laced in a crossing pattern; under tension they hang the hub from the rim.

details.didYouKnow: The uneven tension between the two sides of a rear wheel is a key reason rear wheels go out of true more often than front wheels.
details.howItWorks: The left, non-drive spokes run at a wider angle to the rim because the rear hub is offset, or dished, to fit the cassette on the right. That wider angle means they need much less tension to balance the steep drive-side spokes. Being looser, they are the ones most likely to slacken or fatigue if the wheel is not well built.
details.madeOf: Stainless steel wire, sometimes a thinner butted gauge than the drive side to keep a little more stretch at low tension. Stainless survives road salt and rain.

parts.name: Rear spokes (non-drive side)

parts.description: Stainless spokes laced in a crossing pattern; under tension they hang the hub from the rim.

details.didYouKnow: If you pluck the two sides of a rear wheel, the drive side rings at a noticeably higher pitch because it is so much tighter.
details.howItWorks: The drive-side spokes run almost straight up from the right hub flange, which sits close to the centre to leave room for the cassette. To keep the rim centred they must be pulled much tighter than the left side. They also carry the pedalling torque from the hub out to the rim, which is why they are laced tangentially, crossing each other, rather than radially.
details.madeOf: Stainless steel wire, often a slightly thicker or stronger gauge than the non-drive side because of the higher tension. Steel's fatigue strength matters with every wheel turn.

parts.name: Rear spokes (drive side)

parts.description: Centre of the wheel: an axle on sealed ball bearings, with flanges the spokes hook into.

details.didYouKnow: A freehub lets you stop pedalling while the wheel spins on; early racing bikes often had a fixed gear, so the pedals turned whenever the wheel did.
details.howItWorks: The rear hub holds the axle bearings and carries a freehub body on the drive side, which the cassette slides onto. Inside the freehub, spring-loaded pawls catch a toothed ring when you pedal, and click past it when you coast, which is the ticking sound of a freewheeling bike. Its flanges are set off-centre to make space for the eleven sprockets.
details.madeOf: An aluminium shell and freehub body, steel or titanium pawls and steel bearings. Hard steel is needed where the pawls engage because they take the full pedalling torque.

parts.name: Rear hub

parts.description: Lever-operated skewer that clamps the wheel into the frame, removable without tools.

details.didYouKnow: Shifting onto the smallest sprocket before removing the rear wheel makes it much easier to slip out of the chain and back in again.
details.howItWorks: The rear quick release works like the front one, but it also has to stop the axle being pulled forward in the dropouts by chain tension. Because modern dropouts face downwards, the chain pull mostly pushes the axle up into the slot, and the clamp keeps it there. Removing it lets the wheel drop out once the chain is lifted off the cassette.
details.madeOf: A steel or titanium skewer rod with an alloy cam lever. The rod is slightly longer than the front one to span the wider rear hub.

parts.name: Rear quick release

parts.description: Stack of eleven sprockets from 11 to 28 teeth on the rear hub; the smaller the sprocket, the higher the gear.

details.didYouKnow: In top gear, 50 teeth to 11, one turn of the pedals turns the rear wheel about four and a half times, carrying the bike nearly 10 m.
details.howItWorks: The eleven sprockets slide onto splines on the freehub and are held by a threaded lockring. The rear derailleur moves the chain sideways from one to the next, and ramps and shaped teeth on each sprocket help the chain climb or drop at the right spot. Combined with the two chainrings, it gives 22 gear combinations, though several overlap.
details.madeOf: Hardened steel sprockets for wear resistance, often with the largest ones on an aluminium or plastic carrier to save weight. Steel teeth last much longer than alloy ones under chain wear.

parts.name: Cassette

parts.description: Joins the seat tube to the head tube along the top of the front triangle.

details.didYouKnow: Frame sizes are often quoted from the top tube or seat tube, but two bikes with the same number can fit very differently because of their angles.
details.howItWorks: The top tube closes the front triangle and largely sets the bike's reach, how far forward you stretch to the bars. It carries mostly bending and compression loads between the head tube and seat tube, so it can be thinner than the down tube. On this bike the rear brake cable runs along it.
keyNumbers: About 540 to 560 mm long on a medium frame
Wall thickness under 1 mm in the middle
details.madeOf: Aluminium or steel tube, often thin-walled and butted, then welded and painted. A lighter tube is fine here because the top tube is less heavily loaded.

parts.name: Top tube

parts.description: The frame's biggest tube, from the bottom bracket up to the head tube; it resists the twisting of hard pedalling.

details.didYouKnow: Doubling a tube's diameter at the same wall thickness makes it about eight times stiffer in bending, which is why aluminium frames use fat tubes.
details.howItWorks: The down tube runs diagonally from the head tube to the bottom bracket and resists both twisting from hard pedalling and the steering and braking loads fed in through the fork. Its large diameter matters because a tube's stiffness rises steeply with its width. It often carries the bottle cage bolts and frame decals.
keyNumbers: Typically 35 to 50 mm across on aluminium
Two bottle cage bolts, typically M5
details.madeOf: Usually the thickest tube of an aluminium or steel frame, often ovalised or shaped where it meets the head tube and bottom bracket. Widening the tube gives stiffness without much extra weight.

parts.name: Down tube

parts.description: Runs from the bottom bracket up to the seat post clamp.

details.didYouKnow: 27.2 mm is one of the most common seat post sizes because it suits the bore of classic round frame tubes.
details.howItWorks: The seat tube connects the bottom bracket to the saddle and anchors the seat stays, top tube and front derailleur. The seat post slides inside and is clamped at the top by a collar, often helped by a slot cut in the tube. Its angle sets how far behind the pedals you sit.
details.madeOf: Round aluminium or steel tubing, machined inside the top end so the seat post fits precisely. The round section is needed for the front derailleur band clamp or braze-on.

parts.name: Seat tube

parts.description: Short tube holding the steering bearings that the fork turns in.

details.didYouKnow: A taller head tube lifts the handlebars, so endurance bikes use longer head tubes than race bikes of the same size.
details.howItWorks: The head tube is a short, stout tube that houses the headset bearings, through which the fork steerer passes. Its angle, together with the fork's offset, sets the trail that makes the bike self-centring and stable. It takes large loads from braking and bumps fed in through the fork.
details.madeOf: A thick-walled aluminium or steel tube, machined at both ends to press or seat the bearing cups. It has to stay perfectly round so the bearings run smoothly.

parts.name: Head tube

parts.description: Lower arm of the rear triangle, from the bottom bracket to the rear dropout.

details.didYouKnow: Short chainstays make a bike feel snappier when you stand up and sprint, which is why race bikes keep them as short as tyre clearance allows.
details.howItWorks: The left chainstay runs from the bottom bracket back to the left rear dropout and helps hold the rear axle firmly in line. It carries the rider's weight and braking loads, but unlike the right chainstay it does not take the direct pull of the chain, so it is under less tension. Its length helps set how lively or relaxed the bike feels.
keyNumbers: Tapers to roughly 16 to 20 mm at the dropout
Holds the left side of a 130 mm axle
details.madeOf: Aluminium or steel tube, shaped and tapered towards the dropout, then welded and painted. It can be slimmer than the drive side because it is less heavily loaded.

parts.name: Chainstay (non-drive side)

parts.description: Upper arm of the rear triangle, from the top of the seat tube to the rear dropout.

details.didYouKnow: Designers sometimes make seat stays very thin on purpose, so the rear triangle flexes slightly over bumps and takes the sting out of rough roads.
details.howItWorks: The left seat stay links the top of the seat tube to the left rear dropout, completing one side of the rear triangle. It is quite slender because it mostly takes compression from the rider's weight. Near the top it joins the brake bridge that the rear caliper bolts to, so braking forces pass through it too.
keyNumbers: Joined to the right stay by a brake bridge
details.madeOf: A thin aluminium or steel tube, often curved or flattened to allow a little vertical flex for comfort. Lighter tubing is fine because the loads here are modest.

parts.name: Seat stay (non-drive side)

parts.description: Lower arm of the rear triangle, from the bottom bracket to the rear dropout.

details.didYouKnow: When a chain falls off on the inside, it often wedges between the small chainring and this stay, which is why many bikes carry a chain catcher.
details.howItWorks: The drive-side chainstay sits next to the chain and chainrings and takes the full pull of the chain every pedal stroke. It is usually shaped, dented or dropped to clear the big chainring and the tyre, yet still stiff enough not to flex sideways under power. It often carries a small rubber or metal pad to stop the chain chipping the paint when it slaps.
keyNumbers: Chain pull up to roughly 1,000 to 2,000 N in a hard sprint
details.madeOf: Aluminium or steel tube, often larger or more heavily shaped than the left stay because of the extra chain load. Shaping by hydroforming or crimping makes room for the drivetrain.

parts.name: Chainstay (drive side)

parts.description: Upper arm of the rear triangle, from the top of the seat tube to the rear dropout.

details.didYouKnow: The derailleur hanger is often a separate, softer part designed to bend in a crash, sparing the frame and making a cheap, swappable fix.
details.howItWorks: The right seat stay mirrors the left, running from the seat cluster to the drive-side dropout, which also carries the threaded derailleur hanger. That means it helps hold the rear derailleur in line with the cassette. Together the two stays and the brake bridge keep the rear caliper centred over the rim.
keyNumbers: Derailleur hanger usually bolts on with 1 or 2 screws
details.madeOf: Slim aluminium or steel tube welded to the dropout and seat tube, then painted. The dropout end is solid to anchor the derailleur hanger.

parts.name: Seat stay (drive side)

parts.description: Where the frame tubes meet at the bottom; it holds the bearings the cranks spin on.

details.didYouKnow: On an English-threaded bottom bracket, the drive-side cup has a left-hand thread so pedalling does not slowly unscrew it.
details.howItWorks: The bottom bracket shell is where the seat tube, down tube and both chainstays meet, so it is the most heavily loaded junction on the frame. It holds the bottom bracket bearings, either screwed into threads or pressed in, and the crank axle runs through it. Every pedal stroke twists it from side to side.
keyNumbers: 68 mm wide for a threaded English shell
About 34 to 35 mm inner diameter threaded
Typically 260 to 275 mm above the ground
details.madeOf: A thick-walled aluminium or steel cylinder, machined inside for threads or press-fit bearings. Extra material here gives the stiffness that makes a bike feel efficient under power.

parts.name: Bottom bracket shell

parts.description: One leg of the carbon fork; its forward curve (rake) helps make the steering stable.

details.didYouKnow: Rake and head angle together create trail, the distance the tyre touches the road behind the steering axis, which helps the wheel straighten itself.
details.howItWorks: The left blade runs from the crown down to the left front dropout, and its forward bend adds offset ahead of the steering axis. With rim brakes, this blade sees fairly even loads, since there is no disc caliper pulling on one side. It flexes slightly front to back over bumps, softening road buzz before it reaches your hands.
keyNumbers: About 370 mm from axle to crown
details.madeOf: Carbon fibre sheets laid in a mould at chosen angles and cured under heat and pressure, ending in an aluminium or carbon dropout. Carbon lets designers tune stiffness and damp vibration.

parts.name: Fork blade (left)

parts.description: One leg of the carbon fork; its forward curve (rake) helps make the steering stable.

details.didYouKnow: Carbon forks are usually designed to bend slightly before they break and are tested against fatigue for the equivalent of many thousands of kilometres.
details.howItWorks: The right blade mirrors the left, and the two together clamp the front axle in their dropouts. Both blades have to bend and twist identically, or the front wheel would steer slightly on its own under braking. Lawyer lips on the dropout keep the wheel in place if the quick release is loose.
keyNumbers: Clearance for roughly a 25 to 28 mm tyre
details.madeOf: Carbon fibre composite moulded as part of a one-piece fork with the left blade, crown and steerer, or bonded together. A single mould keeps the two blades matched.

parts.name: Fork blade (right)

parts.description: Joins the two fork blades to the steerer tube.

details.didYouKnow: Braking makes the front of the bike dive, and the fork crown is where that whole bending load concentrates, which is why it is the bulkiest part of the fork.
details.howItWorks: The crown is where the two blades meet the steerer, so it takes the biggest bending loads in the fork when you brake hard. The front brake caliper bolts through a hole in its centre, so braking forces feed straight into it. Its shape also sets the clearance between the tyre and the fork.
keyNumbers: Brake bolt hole about 6 mm diameter
Tyre clearance typically about 4 to 6 mm
Handles braking loads of roughly 1,000 N or more
details.madeOf: Carbon fibre with extra layers for strength, or sometimes an aluminium insert around the brake bolt hole. Extra material here prevents cracking under heavy braking.

parts.name: Fork crown

parts.description: Tube rising from the fork through the head tube; the stem clamps to its top.

details.didYouKnow: Overtightening a stem on a carbon steerer can crush it, so mechanics use a torque wrench and a carbon assembly paste with grit for grip.
details.howItWorks: The steerer is the tube that rises through the head tube, turning in the headset bearings. The stem clamps around its top, and a star nut or expanding plug inside it lets a top cap preload the bearings. Spacers above or below the stem set the bar height before the steerer is cut to length.
keyNumbers: Typically 250 to 300 mm long before cutting
details.madeOf: Carbon fibre or aluminium tube; carbon steerers need an expanding plug instead of a star nut so they are not gouged. Precise outer diameter is critical for the stem clamp.

parts.name: Steerer tube

parts.description: Pair of angular-contact bearings in the head tube that let the fork turn smoothly.

details.didYouKnow: A worn headset can develop indexed steering, where the fork tends to click into the straight-ahead position because the balls have dented their races.
details.howItWorks: Two bearings, one at the top and one at the bottom of the head tube, let the fork rotate while keeping it held firmly in line. Their angled contact surfaces take both the side-to-side and up-and-down loads from steering and bumps. Tightening the top cap squeezes the bearings to remove play before the stem bolts lock it in.
keyNumbers: Steering range up to about 60 degrees each way
details.madeOf: Steel balls in steel or stainless cartridge races, with alloy cups and seals. Hardened steel resists the tiny dents that come from sitting still under impact loads.

parts.name: Headset bearings

parts.description: Clamps the handlebar to the steerer; its length sets how stretched out you ride.

details.didYouKnow: Flipping a stem upside down changes the bar height by a couple of centimetres without buying any new parts.
details.howItWorks: The stem clamps the steerer at one end and the handlebar at the other, with a faceplate held by four bolts. Its length and angle set how far and how low your hands reach, so swapping stems is the quickest way to change a bike's fit. A shorter stem quickens the steering slightly, a longer one calms it.
keyNumbers: Usually about plus or minus 6 degrees
details.madeOf: Forged or machined aluminium alloy, sometimes carbon on high-end bikes. Aluminium is stiff, strong and forgiving of small fitting mistakes.

parts.name: Stem

parts.description: Curved bar giving several hand positions, including the low drops for speed.

details.didYouKnow: At racing speeds, air resistance is the main force a rider fights, and dropping onto the drops can cut drag by roughly 10 to 20%.
details.howItWorks: The drop bar gives three main hand positions: on the tops, on the lever hoods, and down in the curved drops. Riding in the drops lowers your upper body and reduces air drag, while the tops are more relaxed for climbing. Bar tape wraps the bar for grip and comfort, hiding the brake and gear cables underneath.
details.madeOf: An aluminium alloy bar wrapped in fabric, cork or synthetic tape. Aluminium bends and butts easily into shape and is stiff enough for sprinting.

parts.name: Drop handlebar

parts.description: Brake lever that also swings sideways to change gear: the left one shifts the front derailleur.

details.didYouKnow: Integrated brake and gear levers only became standard in the early 1990s; before then road riders shifted with small levers on the down tube.
details.howItWorks: Pulling the left lever back works the front brake through a cable. Pushing the lever sideways pulls the front derailleur cable onto a ratchet to shift to the big ring, while a small inner paddle releases it to drop to the small ring. Its hood also makes the most common place to rest your hands.
keyNumbers: 2 front positions, often plus trim clicks
Lever pivot to blade end about 100 mm
details.madeOf: A plastic or carbon-reinforced body with an aluminium lever blade and steel ratchet parts, covered by a rubber hood. Plastic keeps the body light and comfortable to grip.

parts.name: Brake & shift lever (left)

parts.description: Brake lever that also swings sideways to change gear: the right one shifts the rear derailleur.

details.didYouKnow: Many riders spin the rear derailleur dozens of times more often than the front, so the right lever usually wears out first.
details.howItWorks: The right lever pulls the cable to the rear brake when squeezed back. Sideways swings index the rear derailleur cable one or more clicks at a time to climb the cassette, and the inner paddle releases it to drop to smaller sprockets. An indexing ratchet inside counts each click so every shift lines up exactly with a sprocket.
keyNumbers: Cable pull about 2.7 mm per shift
Shifts up to 3 sprockets in one sweep
details.madeOf: A plastic or composite body housing steel ratchets and springs, with an aluminium blade and a rubber hood. The internal mechanism needs precise steel parts to keep shifts accurate.

parts.name: Brake & shift lever (right)

parts.description: Dual-pivot caliper that squeezes two pads onto the rim; the front brake does most of the stopping.

details.didYouKnow: On hard braking, a road bike's limit is often tipping over the front wheel, not skidding, because the bike is short and the rider sits high.
details.howItWorks: The caliper bolts to the fork crown, and when the cable pulls, its two arms swing on separate pivots to squeeze rubber pads onto the rim. During hard braking the rider's weight shifts forward, so the front brake can provide most of the stopping power. The dual-pivot design gives more leverage than older single-pivot brakes.
keyNumbers: Front brake gives up to about 70 to 90% of stopping force
details.madeOf: Forged aluminium arms with steel pivots and springs, and rubber compound pads in alloy holders. Forged aluminium is stiff, so lever effort goes into the pads rather than bending the arms.

parts.name: Front brake caliper

parts.description: Carbon post that slides into the seat tube to set the saddle height.

details.didYouKnow: Every post has a minimum insertion mark; at least that much must stay inside the frame or the post and seat tube can crack.
details.howItWorks: The seat post slides into the seat tube and is held by a clamp at the frame, so raising or lowering it sets saddle height. A clamp at its top grips the saddle rails, allowing the saddle to be tilted and moved fore and aft. Being long and slender, it flexes a little and absorbs some road vibration.
keyNumbers: Clamp bolts typically about 5 to 6 Nm
details.madeOf: Carbon fibre tube with an aluminium or carbon clamp head. Carbon is light and can be designed to flex slightly for comfort.

parts.name: Seat post

parts.description: Narrow padded saddle on two steel rails; it carries your weight on your sit bones.

details.didYouKnow: Sit bone width varies a lot between riders, so many bike shops measure it by having you sit on a soft gel pad that records the imprint.
details.howItWorks: The saddle supports you on your sit bones while staying narrow enough at the nose for your legs to move freely. Its shell flexes slightly on the rails to take the sting out of bumps. Setting its height, tilt and fore-aft position correctly does more for comfort than the padding itself.
details.madeOf: A nylon or carbon-reinforced shell with a thin foam layer and a synthetic cover, on steel or titanium rails. A firm shell spreads the load better than thick soft padding over long rides.

parts.name: Saddle

parts.description: Caliper on the seat stay bridge, squeezing the rear rim.

details.didYouKnow: In many countries the front brake is on the right lever, but in the UK and some others it is fitted to the left, matching which side traffic passes on.
details.howItWorks: The rear caliper bolts to the bridge between the seat stays and closes its pads on the rear rim when the cable pulls. Because braking moves weight forward, the rear wheel unloads and can lock easily, so it gives less stopping force than the front. It is still useful for scrubbing speed and for braking on loose or wet surfaces.
keyNumbers: Gives roughly 10 to 30% of stopping force
details.madeOf: Forged aluminium arms, steel springs and pivots, rubber compound pads. It is usually identical to the front caliper apart from a shorter mounting bolt.

parts.name: Rear brake caliper

parts.description: 50-tooth front ring for fast riding.

details.didYouKnow: A 50 and 34 tooth pairing is called a compact crankset, a lower-geared alternative to the 53 and 39 rings traditionally used by racers.
details.howItWorks: The big ring bolts to the crank spider and drives the chain when you want speed on flat roads or descents. Its taller teeth have carefully shaped ramps and pins on the inner face that help lift the chain up from the small ring when the front derailleur pushes it across. Paired with the smallest sprocket, it gives the bike's highest gear.
details.madeOf: Machined or stamped aluminium alloy, often hard anodised for wear resistance. Aluminium keeps weight down for such a large disc, and the teeth wear slowly because the load is spread across many of them.

parts.name: Big chainring

parts.description: 34-tooth inner ring for climbing.

details.didYouKnow: Shifting between rings changes your gear by about a third at once, so riders usually follow a front shift with one or two rear shifts to smooth it out.
details.howItWorks: The 34-tooth inner ring gives low gears for climbing, so each pedal turn moves the bike a shorter distance with less effort. When the front derailleur moves inwards, the chain drops off the big ring onto this one. Paired with the 28-tooth sprocket, it gives the bike's lowest gear, just over one wheel turn per pedal turn.
details.madeOf: Steel or aluminium alloy. Steel is heavier but is a common choice for smaller rings because they wear faster, with fewer teeth sharing the load.

parts.name: Small chainring

parts.description: 172.5 mm lever from the pedal to the axle; it carries the chainrings.

details.didYouKnow: The pedal thread on the drive-side crank is a normal right-hand thread, while the other side is left-handed, so pedalling tends to tighten both.
details.howItWorks: The drive-side crank is a lever that turns the force on your pedal into torque on the axle, and its spider carries both chainrings. It is usually bonded or splined permanently onto the axle, so the whole drive side comes out as one piece. Longer cranks give more leverage but a bigger circle for your legs.
keyNumbers: Peak pedal force up to roughly 1,000 N in a sprint
details.madeOf: Forged or hollow aluminium alloy, sometimes carbon on higher-end bikes. Forging aligns the metal grain for strength against millions of fatigue cycles.

parts.name: Crank arm (drive side)

parts.description: Opposite crank, set 180° round so the pedals alternate.

details.didYouKnow: Many power meters sit only in the non-drive crank and simply double the left leg's figure, which is close but not exact, since most people's legs are slightly uneven.
details.howItWorks: The non-drive crank slides onto splines at the other end of the axle and is clamped by pinch bolts or a self-extracting bolt. Set exactly opposite the drive crank, it puts one pedal down as the other comes up, so your legs take turns. Because it carries no chainrings, it passes its torque through the axle to the drive side.
keyNumbers: Set 180 degrees from the drive side
Pinch bolts typically about 12 to 14 Nm
details.madeOf: Forged aluminium alloy, matched in length to the drive crank. The same alloy and shape keep both sides equally stiff and strong.

parts.name: Crank arm (non-drive side)

parts.description: Clipless pedal: a cleat on the shoe clicks into it so you can pull up as well as push down.

details.didYouKnow: Clipless pedals are confusingly named: they clip in, but replaced the older toe clips and straps, which is where the name comes from.
details.howItWorks: A spring-loaded clip on the pedal body grabs a plastic or metal cleat bolted to the rider's shoe. A sharp outward twist of the heel releases it. The pedal body spins on bearings around a steel spindle that screws into the crank with a normal right-hand thread.
details.madeOf: A composite or carbon-reinforced plastic body with a steel or titanium spindle and steel bearings. The body only needs to be stiff, while the spindle must be very strong.

parts.name: Pedal (drive side)

parts.description: The other clipless pedal.

details.didYouKnow: Precession, the slow rolling movement of the bearing on its thread, would loosen a right-hand-threaded left pedal, which is why left pedals use a reverse thread.
details.howItWorks: The non-drive pedal works the same way as its partner, but its spindle has a left-hand thread so that pedalling forces keep tightening it rather than unscrewing it. Most riders unclip this foot first when stopping, so its release tension is often set a little lighter. It is usually marked with an L on the spindle.
details.madeOf: The same composite body, steel spindle and sealed bearings as the drive-side pedal. Bearings are sealed to keep out water and road grit.

parts.name: Pedal (non-drive side)

parts.description: Hollow steel axle on two bearings that joins the cranks through the frame.

details.didYouKnow: A creak that seems to come from the pedals, the saddle or the frame very often turns out to be a dry or loose bottom bracket.
details.howItWorks: The axle passes through the bottom bracket shell and turns on two bearings, one on each side of the frame. Both cranks fix to it, so it carries the twisting force from the non-drive side across to the chainrings. Putting the bearings outside the shell lets the axle be wide and hollow, which is both stiff and light.
keyNumbers: Rotates roughly 80 to 100 times a minute
details.madeOf: A hollow steel or aluminium axle with steel cartridge bearings in alloy cups. Steel axles are strong and cheap; the hollow tube saves weight without much loss of stiffness.

parts.name: Bottom bracket & axle

parts.description: Roller chain of about 110 links; it transmits your pedalling to the rear wheel with very little loss.

details.didYouKnow: Chains do not truly stretch; their pins and rollers wear so the pitch grows, and replacing a chain at about 0.5% wear saves the cassette and chainrings.
details.howItWorks: The chain is a loop of pin-joined links, each with a roller that sits between the teeth of the chainring and sprocket. Only the top run carries load as it pulls the cassette round; the bottom run returns through the derailleur. Its narrow, flexible side plates let it bend sideways to reach every sprocket.
details.madeOf: Hardened steel plates, pins and rollers, often plated or coated against rust. Steel is the only practical material that survives the high contact stresses and constant wear.

parts.name: Chain

parts.description: Spring-loaded arm that guides the chain across the cassette to change gear and keeps the chain tight.

details.didYouKnow: The word derailleur is French for something that derails, which is exactly what it does, deliberately knocking the chain off one sprocket onto the next.
details.howItWorks: The rear derailleur hangs from the frame's dropout and swings on a parallelogram linkage, moving the cage sideways when the cable pulls or a spring pushes back. A second spring rotates the cage backwards to take up slack chain when the chain is on smaller cogs. The limit screws stop it from pushing the chain off either end of the cassette.
keyNumbers: Handles up to about 30 to 32 teeth
Total capacity typically about 33 to 39 teeth
details.madeOf: Aluminium body and cage plates with steel springs and pivots, sometimes carbon parts on lighter models. Aluminium keeps it light while staying stiff enough to shift accurately.

parts.name: Rear derailleur

parts.description: Two small pulleys in the derailleur cage that steer and tension the chain.

details.didYouKnow: Jockey wheels pick up a crust of oily grit faster than almost anything else on a bike, so scraping them clean is a classic part of a quick tune-up.
details.howItWorks: The upper jockey wheel sits close to the cassette and guides the chain onto each sprocket during a shift. The lower wheel, at the end of the sprung cage, keeps tension in the slack bottom run of chain. Both spin quickly on small bushings or bearings and have shaped teeth to keep the chain aligned.
keyNumbers: Spin up to roughly 500 rpm when pedalling hard
details.madeOf: Hard-wearing plastic or ceramic-bearing alloy pulleys. Plastic is quiet, light and gentle on the chain.

parts.name: Jockey wheels

parts.description: Cage on the seat tube that pushes the chain between the two chainrings.

details.didYouKnow: Front shifts work best with light pedal pressure, because the chain must climb or fall between rings that differ by 16 teeth.
details.howItWorks: The front derailleur is a narrow steel cage clamped to the seat tube just above the big chainring. When the cable pulls, a linkage moves the cage outward, and its inner plate pushes the chain sideways until the big ring's pins catch it. Releasing the cable lets a spring move the cage back, and the outer plate nudges the chain onto the small ring.
keyNumbers: Cage typically 1 to 3 mm above the big ring
details.madeOf: A steel cage, which resists wear from the chain rubbing on it, mounted on an aluminium arm and clamp. Steel inner plates stand up to repeated chain contact.

parts.name: Front derailleur

parts.description: Steel cable in a housing along the top tube, pulled by the lever to close the rear caliper.

details.didYouKnow: Brake housing is a tight steel coil that is strong when bent, while gear housing uses lengthwise strands that barely compress, keeping shifts accurate.
details.howItWorks: A stranded steel inner wire slides inside a protective outer housing. When you squeeze the lever, the wire pulls and the housing pushes back, so the force travels round curves to the rear caliper. Along the top tube the bare wire often runs between housing stops, which reduces friction over the long run.
details.madeOf: Stainless steel inner wire inside a plastic-lined, spiral-wound steel housing with a rubber or plastic outer coating. The liner cuts friction and the steel coil resists compression.

parts.name: Rear brake cable

summary: A road bike with a diamond frame, 2×11 derailleur gears and rim brakes: about 8 kg of tubes, wheels and a chain that turn leg power into speed with around 95% efficiency.
